General Theory of Processes - Part 2

This is part 2 of the sequence of blog posts on general theory of processes. For part 1 see here. I will be building upon the content presented there.

Introduction

“Mathematics exists solely for the honour of the human mind.” — Jacobi in a letter to Legendre after the death of Fourier. Fourier had the opinion that the principal aim of mathematics was public utility and explanation of natural phenomena.

We previously discussed Choquet's theory of capacities and its applications in measure theory. The goal of this blog post is to discuss the debut, section and projection theorems in stochastic processes. These theorems form the core of the “general theory of processes”, developed primarily by the Strasbourg school of probability under the tutelage of Paul-André Meyer. At the risk of being overly simplistic, general theory of processes is the study of filtrations and stopping times—martingales will be absent in our discussion.

Unlike part 1 where there were no prerequisites other than basic measure theory, this part assumes a good amount of familiarity with stochastic processes, at the level of (Karatzas and Shreve, 1998a), (Le Gall, 2016). Without that the material here will feel unmotivated and difficult. On the other hand, the theorems proved here are skipped even in advanced courses in stochastic processes as they aren't the most useful for applications, but rather are necessary to fill in gaps if a rigorous treatment is warranted. Nevertheless the theory presented is extremely profound and beautiful, and reading it will be an honour for the mind, if nothing else.

Setting The Stage

Completion of Measure Spaces and Filtrations

Definition 18: A measure space (E,E,μ)(E, \mathscr{E}, \mu)(E,E,μ) is called complete if B∈EB \in \mathscr{E}B∈E and μ(B)=0\mu(B) = 0μ(B)=0 implies that every subset of BBB is in E.\mathscr E.E. We call A⊆EA \subseteq EA⊆E a μ\muμ-negligible or a μ\muμ-null set if there exists B∈EB \in \mathscr EB∈E such that A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B and μ(B)=0.\mu(B) = 0.μ(B)=0. A given statement is said to hold μ\muμ-almost everywhere, or simply μ\muμ-a.e., if the set on which it fails is μ\muμ-negligible.

Thus the measure space (E,E,μ)(E, \mathscr{E}, \mu)(E,E,μ) is complete if and only if every μ\muμ-negligible subset of EEE belongs to E.\mathscr E.E.

Recall that an outer measure on EEE is a function μ∗ ⁣:P(E)→[0,∞]\mu^* \colon \mathfrak{P}(E) \to [0, \infty]μ∗:P(E)→[0,∞] such that

  1. μ∗(∅)=0\mu^*(\varnothing) = 0μ∗(∅)=0,

  2. if A⊆B⊆EA \subseteq B \subseteq EA⊆B⊆E, then μ∗(A)≤μ∗(B)\mu^*(A) \le \mu^*(B)μ∗(A)≤μ∗(B), and

  3. if {An}n∈N\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb N}{An​}n∈N​ is a sequence of subsets of EEE, then

    μ∗(⋃n∈NAn)≤∑n∈Nμ∗(An).\begin{aligned} \mu^*\left( \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb N} A_n \right) \le \sum_{n \in \mathbb N} \mu^*(A_n).\end{aligned}μ∗(n∈N⋃​An​)≤n∈N∑​μ∗(An​).​

Also recall that a subset B⊆EB \subseteq EB⊆E is called μ∗\mu^*μ∗-measurable if

μ∗(A)=μ∗(A∩B)+μ∗(A∩Bc),∀ A⊆E.\begin{aligned} \mu^*(A) = \mu^*(A \cap B) + \mu^*(A \cap B^{\mathsf{c}}), \quad \forall \; A \subseteq E.\end{aligned}μ∗(A)=μ∗(A∩B)+μ∗(A∩Bc),∀A⊆E.​

It is a simple exercise to show that if B⊆EB \subseteq EB⊆E is such that either μ∗(B)=0\mu^*(B) = 0μ∗(B)=0 or μ∗(Bc)=0\mu^*(B^\mathsf{c}) = 0μ∗(Bc)=0, then BBB is μ∗\mu^*μ∗-measurable. Finally, recall that if Mμ∗\mathscr{M}_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​ denotes the collection of all μ∗\mu^*μ∗-measurable subsets of EEE, then Mμ∗\mathscr{M}_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​ is a σ\sigmaσ-algebra, and the restriction of μ∗\mu^*μ∗ to Mμ∗\mathscr{M}_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​ is a measure on Mμ∗.\mathscr{M}_{\mu^*}.Mμ∗​. Therefore, it follows that the measure space (E,Mμ∗,μ∗)(E, \mathscr{M}_{\mu^*}, \mu^*)(E,Mμ∗​,μ∗) is complete. In particular, the Lebesgue measure on the σ\sigmaσ-algebra of Lebesgue subsets of R\mathbb RR is complete. It can be shown that the restriction of Lebesgue measure to the σ\sigmaσ-algebra of Borel subsets of R\mathbb RR is not complete. We next discuss a result that allows us to complete any measure space.

A very nice property that holds if we assume that the measure space (E,E,μ)(E, \mathscr{E}, \mu)(E,E,μ) is complete is that if fff and ggg are real-valued functions defined EEE such that fff is measurable and and f=gf = gf=g holds μ\muμ-a.e., then ggg is also measurable. by our assumptions. Thus, {f=g}={f≠g}c∈E\{f = g\} = \{f \neq g \}^\mathsf{c} \in \mathscr E{f=g}={f=g}c∈E, and
{g∈B}=({f∈B}∩{f=g})∪A∈E\begin{aligned} \{g \in B\} = \left(\{f \in B\} \cap \{f = g\}\right) \cup A \in \mathscr E\end{aligned}{g∈B}=({f∈B}∩{f=g})∪A∈E​
allows us to conclude that ggg is measurable.

The above property can fail if the measure space is not complete. Similar problems can arise in the study of stochastic processes, and therefore completeness assumptions are made. Stochastic Processes

For our purposes, a stochastic process is simply a collection of real-valued random variables X={Xt}t≥0X = \{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}X={Xt​}t≥0​ on (Ω,F).(\Omega, \mathcal{F}).(Ω,F). The sample paths of XXX are the mapping [0,∞)∋t↦Xt(ω)∈R[0, \infty) \ni t \mapsto X_t( \omega) \in \mathbb R[0,∞)∋t↦Xt​(ω)∈R obtained when fixing ω∈Ω.\omega \in \Omega.ω∈Ω.

We need terminology to talk about when two stochastic processes are the “same”.

Definition 19: Consider two stochastic process X={Xt}t≥0X = \left\{ X_t\right\}_{t \ge 0}X={Xt​}t≥0​ and Y={Yt}t≥0Y = \left\{ Y_t\right\}_{t \ge 0}Y={Yt​}t≥0​ defined on the same probability space (Ω,F,P).(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}).(Ω,F,P). We say

  1. XXX and YYY have the same finite-dimensional distributions if, for any integer n≥1n \ge 1n≥1, real numbers 0≤t1<t2<⋯<tn<∞,0 \le t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_n < \infty,0≤t1​<t2​<⋯<tn​<∞, and A∈B(Rn)A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb R^n)A∈B(Rn), we have

P{(Xt1,…,Xtn)∈A}=P{(Yt1,…,Ytn)∈A};\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}\{(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n}) \in A\} = \mathbb{P}\{(Y_{t_1}, \ldots, Y_{t_n}) \in A\};\end{aligned}P{(Xt1​​,…,Xtn​​)∈A}=P{(Yt1​​,…,Ytn​​)∈A};​

  1. YYY is a modification or a version of XXX if, for every t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞), we have P{Xt=Yt}=1;\mathbb{P}\{X_t = Y_t\} = 1;P{Xt​=Yt​}=1;

  2. XXX and YYY are indistinguishable if almost all their sample paths agree, i.e.,

    P{Xt=Yt ∀ t∈[0,∞)}=1.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}\{X_t = Y_t \;\; \forall \, t \in [0, \infty)\} = 1.\end{aligned}P{Xt​=Yt​∀t∈[0,∞)}=1.​
    The set {Xt=Yt ∀ t∈[0,∞)}\{X_t = Y_t \;\; \forall \, t \in [0, \infty)\}{Xt​=Yt​∀t∈[0,∞)} is measurable because of our completeness assumption.

We will need to make stronger measurability assumptions for the random variables {Xt}t≥0\{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}{Xt​}t≥0​ than just assuming that each XtX_tXt​ is measurable.

Definition 20: A stochastic process X={Xt}t≥0X = \{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}X={Xt​}t≥0​ is called

  1. adapted, if XtX_tXt​ is Ft\mathcal{F}_tFt​-measurable for every t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞);

  2. measurable, if the mapping [0,∞)×Ω∋(t,ω)↦Xt(ω)∈R\begin{aligned} [0, \infty) \times \Omega \ni (t,\omega) \mapsto X_t(\omega) \in \mathbb R\end{aligned}[0,∞)×Ω∋(t,ω)↦Xt​(ω)∈R​ is B([0,∞))⊗F\mathcal{B}([0, \infty)) \otimes \mathcal{F}B([0,∞))⊗F-measurable, when R\mathbb RR is endowed with its Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra;

  3. progressively measurable, if for every t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞) the mapping

    [0,t]×Ω∋(s,ω)↦Xs(ω)∈R\begin{aligned} [0,t] \times \Omega \ni (s,\omega) \mapsto X_s(\omega) \in \mathbb R\end{aligned}[0,t]×Ω∋(s,ω)↦Xs​(ω)∈R​
    is B([0,t])⊗Ft\mathcal{B}([0,t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_tB([0,t])⊗Ft​-measurable, when R\mathbb RR is endowed with its Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

Recall that every progressively measurable process is both measurable and adapted; and every adapted process with right-continuous or with left-continuous paths, is progressively measurable (Karatzas and Shreve, 1998a), (Le Gall, 2016). On the other hand, we have the following result due to Meyer (1966).

Theorem 12: Every measurable and adapted process X={Xt}t≥0X = \{X_t\} _ {t \ge 0}X={Xt​}t≥0​ has a progressively measurable modification Y={Yt}t≥0.Y = \{Y_t\} _ {t \ge 0}.Y={Yt​}t≥0​.

Consider the space L0\mathbb{L}^0L0 of equivalence classes of measurable functions f:Ω→Rf : \Omega \to \mathbb Rf:Ω→R, and endow it with the topology of convergence in probability, for example with the pseudo-metrics ρ(f,g)=E(1∧∣f−g∣)\rho(f, g) = \mathbb E (1 \wedge |f-g|)ρ(f,g)=E(1∧∣f−g∣) or ρ(f,g)=E(∣f−g∣1+∣f−g∣).\rho(f,g) = \mathbb E \left( \frac{|f-g|}{1 + |f-g|} \right).ρ(f,g)=E(1+∣f−g∣∣f−g∣​). Recall that if a sequence {fn}n∈N⊆L0\{f_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathbb{L}^0{fn​}n∈N​⊆L0 satisfies ∑n∈Nρ(fn,fn+1)<∞,\sum _ {n \in \mathbb N} \rho(f _ n, f _ {n+1}) < \infty,∑n∈N​ρ(fn​,fn+1​)<∞, then it converges in probability “fast”, thus also almost surely.

Every process Y={Yt}t≥0Y = \{Y_t\} _ {t \ge 0}Y={Yt​}t≥0​ can be thought of as a mapping from [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) into L0\mathbb{L}^0L0, which associates to each element in [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) the equivalence class Yt\mathcal{Y} _ tYt​ of Yt.Y_t.Yt​. Consider now the collection H\mathscr{H}H of processes YYY such that the mapping [0,∞)∋t↦Yt∈L0[0, \infty) \ni t \mapsto \mathcal{Y}_t \in \mathbb{L}^0[0,∞)∋t↦Yt​∈L0 satisfies

  1. it takes values in a separable subspace of L0\mathbb{L}^0L0;

  2. under it, the inverse image of every open ball of L0\mathbb{L}^0L0 is a Borel subset of [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞); and

  3. it is the uniform limit of a sequence of simple measurable functions with values in the space L0.\mathbb{L}^0.L0.

Then note that property 3 implies the other two, and that conversely, properties 1 and 2 together imply property 3, because a real-valued function is measurable if and only if it is the increasing limit of a sequence of simple measurable functions.

Next, note that H\mathscr{H}H is a real vector space on account of property 3, and is closed under sequential pointwise convergence on account of properties 1 and 2. It is easy to see that H\mathscr{H}H contains all processes of the form Y(t,ω)=K(t)ξ(ω)Y(t,\omega) = K(t) \xi(\omega)Y(t,ω)=K(t)ξ(ω), where KKK is the indicator of an interval in [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) and ξ:Ω→R\xi : \Omega \to \mathbb Rξ:Ω→R is a bounded measurable function. Thus, monotone class theorem implies H\mathscr{H}H contains all bounded measurable processes. Now using a standard slicing argument it is easily seen that every measurable process YYY has properties 1, 2 and 3.

Consider now a measurable and adapted process X={Xt}t≥0.X = \{X_t\} _ {t \ge 0}.X={Xt​}t≥0​. Definition 22: A random variable T:Ω→[0,∞]T : \Omega \to [0, \infty]T:Ω→[0,∞] is called a stopping time if {T≤t}∈Ft\{T \le t\} \in \mathcal{F}_t{T≤t}∈Ft​ for all t∈[0,∞).t \in [0, \infty).t∈[0,∞).

{T≤t}=⋂q∈Q,t<q<s{T<q}∈Fs.\begin{aligned} \{T \le t\} = \bigcap_{\substack{q \in \mathbb{Q}, \, t < q < s}} \{T < q\} \in \mathcal{F}_s.\end{aligned}{T≤t}=q∈Q,t<q<s​⋂​{T<q}∈Fs​.​

T∧S, T∨S and T+S.\begin{aligned} T \wedge S,\, T \vee S \text{ and } T+S.\end{aligned}T∧S,T∨S and T+S.​

{XT∧t}t≥0\begin{aligned} \left\{X_{T \wedge t}\right\}_{t \ge 0}\end{aligned}{XT∧t​}t≥0​​
is F\mathbb{F}F-progressively measurable.

Predictable Stopping Times

A very important result states that every stopping time is the decreasing limit of a sequence of discrete stopping time. More concretely, if TTT is a stopping time, and we define

Tn(ω)={k2−non {k−12n≤T<k2n}T(ω)on {T=∞},\begin{aligned} T_n(\omega) = \begin{cases} k 2^{-n} &\text{on } \left\{\frac{k-1}{2^n} \le T < \frac{k}{2^n}\right\} \\ T(\omega) &\text{on } \{T = \infty\}, \end{cases}\end{aligned}Tn​(ω)={k2−nT(ω)​on {2nk−1​≤T<2nk​}on {T=∞},​​

for n,k∈N,n,k \in \mathbb N,n,k∈N, then each TnT_nTn​ is a discrete stopping time and we have Tn↓T.T_n \downarrow T.Tn​↓T. When can we approximate a stopping with an increasing sequence of stopping times? Of course, being able to do that means that our stopping time is a very special one. We give a name to such stopping times.

Definition 24: A stopping time TTT is called predictable, if there exists an increasing (“announcing”) sequence {Tn}n∈N\{T_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{Tn​}n∈N​ of stopping times with T=lim⁡n∈N↑TnT = \lim _ {n \in \mathbb N} \uparrow T_nT=limn∈N​↑Tn​, and Tn<TT_n < TTn​<T holds on the set {T>0}\{T > 0\}{T>0} for all n∈N.{n \in \mathbb N}.n∈N.

Note {T≤t}=⋂n∈N{Tn≤t}∈F(t)\{T \le t\} = \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} \{T_n \le t\} \in \mathcal{F}(t){T≤t}=⋂n∈N​{Tn​≤t}∈F(t) and therefore if in the definition above we had not required TTT to be a stopping time, it would still be a stopping time. A canonical example of a predictable stopping time is the first time Brownian motion WWW hits or exceeds a certain level b.b.b. It is announced by the sequence of first times WWW hits or exceeds the levels b−1/nb - 1/nb−1/n, for n∈N.{n \in \mathbb N}.n∈N. In fact, we have (taken from (Almost Sure blog)):

Theorem 13: Let XXX be a continuous adapted process and bbb be a real number. Then
T=inf⁡{t∈[0,∞) : X(t)≥b}\begin{aligned} T = \inf \{t \in [0, \infty)\,:\,X(t) \ge b\}\end{aligned}T=inf{t∈[0,∞):X(t)≥b}​
is a predictable stopping time.
Let
Tn=inf⁡{t∈[0,∞) : X(t)≥b−1/n},\begin{aligned} T_n = \inf \{t \in [0, \infty)\,:\,X(t) \ge b - 1/n\},\end{aligned}Tn​=inf{t∈[0,∞):X(t)≥b−1/n},​

Optional and Predictable Processes

Definition 26: The predictable σ\sigmaσ-algebra, denoted by P\mathscr{P}P, is the smallest σ\sigmaσ-algebra on [0,∞)×Ω[0, \infty) \times \Omega[0,∞)×Ω with respect to which left-continuous F\mathbb{F}F-adapted processes are measurable. A stochastic process is said to predictable if it is P\mathscr{P}P-measurable.
Definition 27: The optional σ\sigmaσ-algebra, denoted by O\mathscr{O}O, is the smallest σ\sigmaσ-algebra on [0,∞)×Ω[0, \infty) \times \Omega[0,∞)×Ω with respect to which right-continuous F\mathbb{F}F-adapted processes are measurable. A stochastic process is said to optional if it is O\mathscr{O}O-measurable.

Since all right-continuous or left-continuous adapted processes are progressively measurable, all optional or predictable processes are adapted. We need the concept of stochastic intervals to ease some notation and see some examples of optional and predictable sets.

Properties of Debuts

Recall the setting of section "Measurable Section" from part 1. We showed there that if A∈B([0,∞))⊗F,A \in \mathcal{B}([0, \infty)) \otimes \mathcal{F},A∈B([0,∞))⊗F, then we can define a measurable mapping T:Ω→[0,∞]T : \Omega \to [0, \infty]T:Ω→[0,∞] such that for all ω∈π(A)\omega \in \pi(A)ω∈π(A) we have (T(ω),ω)∈A(T(\omega), \omega) \in A(T(ω),ω)∈A, or stated more succinctly, ⟦T⟧⊆A.\llbracket T \rrbracket \subseteq A.[[T]]⊆A. Now, what if we want something stronger, say, TTT should be a stopping time? As we will see, we will have to make stronger assumptions on the set AAA and even then if we want TTT to be a stopping time we will have to let go of the nice property that {T<∞}=π(A).\{T < \infty\}= \pi(A).{T<∞}=π(A).

But first, we need to prove a certain property of debuts which we will need in proving the aforementioned section theorem, and that's the goal of this section.

It isn't difficult to see that P\mathscr{P}P coincides with the mosaic generated by the paving on [0,∞)×Ω[0, \infty) \times \Omega[0,∞)×Ω that consists of finite unions of stochastic intervals of the form ⟦S,T⟧\llbracket S,T \rrbracket[[S,T]], where S,T∈S(P).S,T \in \mathfrak{S}^{(\mathscr{P})}.S,T∈S(P). Generalizing this, let us consider a collection A\mathfrak{A}A (A\mathfrak{A}A is A in fraktur font) of stopping times that contains 000 and ∞\infty∞, and which is closed under a.s. equality and under finitely many lattice operations (∧\wedge∧ and ∨\vee∨). We denote by J:={⟦U,V⟦ : S,T∈A}\mathcal{J} := \{\llbracket U,V \llbracket\,:\,S,T \in \mathfrak{A}\}J:={[[U,V[[:S,T∈A}, and by T\mathcal{T}T the collection of finite unions of elements of J.\mathcal{J}.J.

Simple observations like ⟦S,T⟦c=⟦0,S⟦ ∪ ⟦T,∞⟦\llbracket S,T \llbracket^\mathsf{c} = \llbracket 0, S \llbracket \, \cup \, \llbracket T, \infty \llbracket[[S,T[[c=[[0,S[[∪[[T,∞[[ or ⟦S,T⟦ ∩ ⟦U,V⟦=⟦S∨U,(S∨U)∨(T∧V)⟦\llbracket S,T \llbracket \, \cap \, \llbracket U,V \llbracket = \llbracket S \vee U, (S \vee U) \vee (T \wedge V) \llbracket[[S,T[[∩[[U,V[[=[[S∨U,(S∨U)∨(T∧V)[[ can be used to show that J\mathcal{J}J is a paving on [0,∞)×Ω[0, \infty) \times \Omega[0,∞)×Ω and T\mathcal{T}T is an algebra on [0,∞)×Ω.[0, \infty) \times \Omega.[0,∞)×Ω.

For more structure, let us impose the following properties on the collection A\mathfrak{A}A:

Applications of Section Theorems

Recall the measurable graph theorem (Theorem 8 in part 1) which implies that a map T:Ω→[0,∞]T : \Omega \to [0, \infty]T:Ω→[0,∞] is measurable if and only if its graph ⟦T⟧\llbracket T \rrbracket[[T]] is measurable. We also have the following neat result:

Theorem 20: A random variable T:Ω→[0,∞]T : \Omega \to [0, \infty]T:Ω→[0,∞] is a stopping time (respectively, a predictable stopping time), if and only if its graph ⟦T⟧\llbracket T \rrbracket[[T]] is an optional (respectively, predictable) set.

The necessity follows from the characterization of O\mathscr{O}O and P\mathscr{P}P in Lemma 8.

In the optional case, sufficiency follows from Theorem 14 and the fact that O⊆P⋆.\mathscr{O} \subseteq \mathscr{P}_\star.O⊆P⋆​.

For the sufficiency in the predictable case, suppose ⟦T⟧\llbracket T \rrbracket[[T]] is predictable. Apply Predictable Section theorem (Theorem 18) for A=⟦T⟧A = \llbracket T \rrbracketA=[[T]] to construct a sequence {Tn}n∈N\{T_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{Tn​}n∈N​ of predictable stopping times such that

⟦Tn⟧⊆⟦T⟧ and P(T<∞)≤P(Tn<∞)+2−n,∀ n∈N.\begin{aligned} \llbracket T_n \rrbracket \subseteq \llbracket T \rrbracket \text{ and } \mathbb{P}(T < \infty) \le \mathbb{P}(T_n < \infty) + 2^{-n}, \quad \forall \; {n \in \mathbb N}.\end{aligned}[[Tn​]]⊆[[T]] and P(T<∞)≤P(Tn​<∞)+2−n,∀n∈N.​

T=lim⁡n∈N↑Tn=sup⁡n∈NTn\begin{aligned} T = \lim _ {n \in \mathbb N} \uparrow T_n = \sup _ {n \in \mathbb N} T_n\end{aligned}T=n∈Nlim​↑Tn​=n∈Nsup​Tn​​
is predictable: if {Tnm}m∈N\{T_n^m\} _ {m \in \mathbb N}{Tnm​}m∈N​ announces TnT_nTn​, then
τn=max⁡{Tjk : j,k≤n}\begin{aligned} \tau_n = \max \{T_j^k \,: \, j,k \le n\}\end{aligned}τn​=max{Tjk​:j,k≤n}​

Projection Theorems

To motivate optional and predictable projections, let us start with a fundamental problem in filtering theory: Assume an underlying complete probability space (Ω,F,P).(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}).(Ω,F,P). There is an underlying signal X={Xt}t≥0X = \{X_t\} _ {t \ge 0}X={Xt​}t≥0​ which is modelled as a stochastic process and which we are interested in studying. Our observation process has noise and therefore instead of observing XXX we observe a process Y={Yt}t≥0Y = \{Y_t\} _ {t \ge 0}Y={Yt​}t≥0​ such that

Yt=ft(Xt,Wt),\begin{aligned} Y_t = f_t(X_t, W_t),\end{aligned}Yt​=ft​(Xt​,Wt​),​
for Wiener process W={Wt}t≥0.W = \{W_t\}_{t \ge 0}.W={Wt​}t≥0​. Therefore, it makes sense to define F={Ft}t≥0\mathbb{F} = \{\mathcal{F}_t\} _ {t \ge 0}F={Ft​}t≥0​ to be the minimal augmented filtration generated by Y.Y.Y. The problem, then, is to compute an estimate for XXX based on the observable data at time ttt, viz. Ft.\mathcal{F}_t.Ft​.

We could look at Zt:=E(Xt∣Ft),\begin{aligned} Z_t := \mathbb{E} \left( X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right),\end{aligned}Zt​:=E(Xt​∣Ft​),​ as an estimate for XtX_tXt​ at each time t≥0.t \ge 0.t≥0. The process Z={Zt}t≥0Z = \{Z_t\}_{t \ge 0}Z={Zt​}t≥0​ is, of course, adapted. However, since conditional expectation is defined only up to P\mathbb{P}P-a.s., what version of ZZZ should we choose? (9) does not fix the paths of the process ZZZ, which requires specifying its values at the uncountable set of time in [0,∞).[0, \infty).[0,∞). We would be very lucky if it were possible for us to choose a version of ZZZ such that (9) holds not only for all t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞) but also for all finite stopping times. And indeed this is possible! This is part of the statement of the optional projection theorem.

On the other hand, if we want an estimate of XXX based on observable data before time ttt, then our estimate would be

Zt=E(Xt∣Ft−)\begin{aligned} Z_t = \mathbb{E}(X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-})\end{aligned}Zt​=E(Xt​∣Ft−​)​
where recall Ft−:=σ(⋃s<tFs).\mathcal{F}_{t-} := \sigma\left(\bigcup _ {s < t} \mathcal{F}_s\right).Ft−​:=σ(⋃s<t​Fs​). Again it is possible to choose a version of ZZZ such that this equality holds not only for all t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞) but also for all finite predictable stopping times, and this is part of the statement of the predictable projection theorem.

Theorem 22 [Optional and Predictable Projections]: Let XXX be a bounded, measurable (though not necessarily adapted) process.

  1. There is a unique, modulo indistinguishability, optional process XoX^oXo, called optional projection of XXX, that satisfies for all stopping times T∈ST \in \mathfrak{S}T∈S the identity

E(XT1{T<∞}∣FT)=XTo1{T<∞}.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left( X_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}} \mid \mathcal{F}_T \right) = X^o_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}}.\end{aligned}E(XT​1{T<∞}​∣FT​)=XTo​1{T<∞}​.​

  1. There is a unique, modulo indistinguishability, predictable process XpX^pXp, called predictable projection of XXX, that satisfies for all predictable stopping times T∈S(P)T \in \mathfrak{S}^{(\mathscr{P})}T∈S(P) the identity

E(XT1{T<∞}∣FT−)=XTp1{T<∞}.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left( X_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{T-} \right) = X^p_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}}.\end{aligned}E(XT​1{T<∞}​∣FT−​)=XTp​1{T<∞}​.​

Remarks:

  1. Taking expectations in (10) we get E(XT1{T<∞})=E(XTo1{T<∞})\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E} \left(X_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}}\right) = \mathbb{E} \left(X_T^o \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}}\right)\end{aligned}E(XT​1{T<∞}​)=E(XTo​1{T<∞}​)​ for all stopping times T∈S.T \in \mathfrak{S}.T∈S. Now suppose (12) holds for all stopping times T∈S.T \in \mathfrak{S}.T∈S. Fix an arbitrary stopping time S∈SS \in \mathfrak{S}S∈S and a set A∈FSA \in \mathcal{F}_SA∈FS​, and write (12) for T=SAT = S_AT=SA​ to get

    E(XS1{S<∞}1A)=E(XSo1{S<∞}1A).\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E} \left(X_S \mathbf{1}_{\{S < \infty\}} \mathbf{1}_A\right) = \mathbb{E} \left(X_S^o \mathbf{1}_{\{S < \infty\}} \mathbf{1}_A\right).\end{aligned}E(XS​1{S<∞}​1A​)=E(XSo​1{S<∞}​1A​).​
    But this immediately implies (10) for stopping time S.S.S. Therefore, requiring (10) to hold for all stopping times is equivalent to requiring (12) to hold for for all stopping times.

  2. Similarly, requiring (11) to hold for all predictable stopping times is equivalent to requiring E(XT1{T<∞})=E(XTp1{T<∞})\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left( X_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}} \right) = \mathbb{E}\left(X^p_T \mathbf{1}_{\{T < \infty\}}\right)\end{aligned}E(XT​1{T<∞}​)=E(XTp​1{T<∞}​)​ to hold for all predictable stopping times.

  3. Operators o^oo and p^pp are linear operators, i.e., for bounded, measurable processes X,YX,YX,Y and a,b∈Ra,b \in \mathbb Ra,b∈R,

    (aX+bY)o=aXo+bYo, and(aX+bY)p=aXp+bYp,\begin{aligned} (aX + bY)^o &= a X^o + bY^o, \text{ and} \\ (aX + bY)^p &= a X^p + bY^p,\end{aligned}(aX+bY)o(aX+bY)p​=aXo+bYo, and=aXp+bYp,​
    as can be easily verified by using the properties of conditional expectation. The formulation of (12) and (13) makes it obvious that (Xo)o=Xo\left(X^o\right)^o = X^o(Xo)o=Xo and (Xp)p=Xp.\left(X^p\right)^p = X^p.(Xp)p=Xp. This explains the terminology of “projection”.

[of Theorem 22] Uniqueness is immediate from Theorem 21, so let's focus on existence, first for optional projection and then for predictable projection.

  1. We will employ the monotone class theorem for functions. We need a simple class of processes for which finding an optional projection is easy to summon. To this end, consider the processes of the form

    Xt(ω)=1B(ω)1[u,v)(t),0≤u<v<∞ and B∈F.\begin{aligned} X_t(\omega) = \mathbf{1}_{B}(\omega) \mathbf{1}_{[u,v)}(t), \quad 0 \le u < v < \infty \text{ and } B \in \mathcal{F}.\end{aligned}Xt​(ω)=1B​(ω)1[u,v)​(t),0≤u<v<∞ and B∈F.​
    We claim that the candidate for the optional projection is
    Xto(ω):=Mt(ω)1[u,v)(t),\begin{aligned} X^o_t(\omega) := M_t(\omega) \mathbf{1}_{[u,v)}(t),\end{aligned}Xto​(ω):=Mt​(ω)1[u,v)​(t),​
    where MMM is the right-continuous version of the bounded, thus also uniformly integrable, martingale E(1B∣Ft)\mathbb{E}\left( \mathbf{1}_B \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right)E(1B​∣Ft​) (see (Karatzas and Shreve, 1998a), (Le Gall, 2016) for the proof of existence of such a martingale; it is here that the usual conditions on the filtration F\mathbb{F}F become crucial).

    With these choices and an arbitrary stopping time TTT, the left-hand side of (12) becomes P{B∩{u≤T<v}}\mathbb{P}\{B \cap \{u \le T < v\}\}P{B∩{u≤T<v}}, whereas optional stopping theorem (Karatzas and Shreve, 1998a), (Le Gall, 2016) shows that its right-hand side is

    E(E(1B∣FT)∣1[u,v)(T)).\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E} \left( \mathbb{E} \left(\mathbf{1}_B \mid \mathcal{F}_T \right) \mid \mathbf{1}_{[u,v)}(T) \right).\end{aligned}E(E(1B​∣FT​)∣1[u,v)​(T)).​
    Recalling now that TTT is FT\mathcal{F}_TFT​-measurable shows that the two sides are equal.

    Finally, use linearity and monotone class arguments to establish existence for arbitrary bounded, measurable X.X.X.

  2. Similar ideas work in the predictable case. We first consider processes of the form

    Xt(ω)=1B(ω)1(u,v](t),0≤u<v<∞ and B∈F.\begin{aligned} X_t(\omega) = \mathbf{1}_{B}(\omega) \mathbf{1}_{(u,v]}(t), \quad 0 \le u < v < \infty \text{ and } B \in \mathcal{F}.\end{aligned}Xt​(ω)=1B​(ω)1(u,v]​(t),0≤u<v<∞ and B∈F.​
    We claim that the candidate for the predictable projection is
    Xtp(ω):=Mt−(ω)1(u,v](t),\begin{aligned} X^p_t(\omega) := M_{t-}(\omega) \mathbf{1}_{(u,v]}(t),\end{aligned}Xtp​(ω):=Mt−​(ω)1(u,v]​(t),​
    where Mt−M_{t-}Mt−​ is the left-continuous version of the martingale MMM defined previously. Again using FT−\mathcal{F}_{T-}FT−​-measurability of TTT we see the two sides of (13) are equal. Monotone class arguments now allow us to finish the proof.

We end our discussion with a result on time change. We call it a “time change” because given an adapted increasing process AAA with right-continuous paths and A0=0,A_0 = 0,A0​=0, we imagine a clock which runs according to AAA in the sense that at time ttt this clock shows time At.A_t.At​.
